documentation.range:
Widely distributed across Africa south of the Sahara, from Senegal, The Gambia, and Guinea-Bissau eastwards through the Sahelian zone to Cameroon, South Sudan, Sudan and Eritrea, south through western Somalia and the Rift Valley to much of southern Africa, although is scarce below 28 degrees latitude.

The bulk of the population is found in East Africa, where is is common to abundant even in some large cities. In Uganda, the switch to urban habits has driven a rapid increase in the population (Pomeroy and Kibuule 2017, 2021). At the start of the 20th century the species was rare in Uganda and restricted to savanna in the west of the country due to overhunting for their feathers for the fashion trade (Jackson and Sclater 1938). With the decline in demand for feathers to adorn clothing in Europe numbers increased, but the rate of increase accelerated with the species’ switch to human-commensal habits (Brown et al. 1982). Marabou first bred in Kampala in 1968, with 10 pairs, with numbers rapidly increasing to around 700 in 2000-2001, over 1,100 pairs in 2007-2008 (Ssemmanda and Pomeroy 2014) and up to a peak of 1,233 breeding pairs in 2016-2017 (Pomeroy and Kibuule 2017, 2021). Numbers counted fluctuate however, with fewer than 800 pairs again in 2012-2013 and recently down to around 900 in the 2021-2022 breeding season from the peak in 2016-2017 (Pomeroy and Kibuule 2021).

The species is also increasing across the Gorongosa landscape in Mozambique, with 380 nests in 2019 a rapid increase since the first monitoring in 2016 (Stalmans et al. 2020).

It is known to breed at relatively few and scattered sites across all of Zimbabwe, Eswatini, South Africa, Botswana and Namibia, where colonies are also generally small (Anderson 2005, Simmons et al. 2015). Numbers are increasing in the Okavango Delta in Botswana (Francis et al. 2021) where 50-200 nests were reported by Tarboton (2001). 

In West Africa there has been a significant contraction of the range and reduction in abundance, especially in Nigeria and Mali (Gula and Barlow 2023). It continues to breed in The Gambia, Benin, Cameroon and Chad, but no longer does so in Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Mali and Nigeria; there is uncertainty for other countries but numbers breeding cannot be large (Gula and Barlow 2023). There have been no reports of nesting in Mali for over 40 years, and despite good sized colonies assumed to be active in adjacent Cameroon the last reported nesting in Nigeria was in 1991 (Gula and Barlow 2023). In Cameroon, at least five nesting colonies were present in villages in the Waza-Logone floodplain and Waza National Park in the 1990s, with over 200 nests in some (Gula and Barlow 2023). One colony, of 500 nests, was reported to have been abandoned in 2002 following chick harvest for food (Scholte 2006). Continued breeding by significant numbers is assumed following a record of 500+ individuals in Nigeria in the immediate post-breeding period in 2021 (Ringim et al. 2021), though this may also potentially hint at further significant disturbance events in Cameroon. There are few recent records from Niger, where the species previously bred, but in Benin it continues to breed in declining numbers at Pendjari National Park (Dowsett-Lemaire and Dowsett 2019). Few active colonies are now known in The Gambia, with fewer than 60 nests recorded in recent years, down from over 200 in the late 1980s, while numbers breeding in Senegal are very low and the last nesting report was in 2007 (Gula and Barlow 2023).

The loss of former breeding range in West Africa is thought to outweigh any slight increase in occupied area resulting from the increases in other parts of the range, hence a continuing decline in the AOO is inferred.
documentation.population:
An estimate of 200,000-500,000 individuals was made based on expert opinion in 2006 (Dodman 2006). This remains the current population estimate (Wetlands International 2024), but is highly uncertain. An exceptionally high count of 360,000 made in 1979 for the Sudd, in South Sudan is considered likely inaccurate, given that it was based on an extrapolation of a count in one place to the entire area while the congregatory nature of the species suggests even abundance across the Sudd is highly unlikely. However there has been no effort to generate an accurate estimate of the likely large numbers that do occur in South Sudan, or to determine if very large concentrations may occur seasonally.

The bulk of the population is found in East Africa, and it is common from Ethiopia and western Somalia through Kenya, Uganda, northern Tanzania, but although it is widely recorded in southern Africa it is known to breed at only a few widely scattered sites (Anderson 2005). Dispersal distances can be very large, up to 1,500 km (Monadjem et al. 2008), and the ease of detection of such a large bird means that a single individual can generate many records across a large area, and care is needed not to overestimate the total population size. This said, it is clear that the abundance of the species across a large part of East Africa and at least some of Central Africa means that the population is certainly large.
documentation.habitats: Behaviour This species is sedentary or locally nomadic (Hancock et al. 1992, del Hoyo et al. 1992). Populations in the north and south generally move towards the equator after breeding and other populations making dispersive movements in relation to water availablity (del Hoyo et al. 1992) or prey abundance (Hancock et al. 1992). In the tropics the species begins to breed in the dry season, but in the equatorial zone the timing of breeding is more variable (del Hoyo et al. 1992). It breeds in colonies numbering from 20-60 up to several thousand pairs and often nests with other species (del Hoyo et al. 1992). When not breeding the species often remains gregarious, feeding in groups and gathering at night in communal roosts of up to 1,000 individuals (Hancock et al. 1992), sometimes considerably more (Gula and Pomeroy 2023). It may also associate with herds of large mammals in order to catch insects disturbed by their movements (del Hoyo et al. 1992). Habitat It inhabits open dry savannas, grasslands, swamps, riverbanks, lake shores and receding pools (del Hoyo et al. 1992) where fish are concentrated (Hancock et al. 1992), typically foraging in and around fishing villages (del Hoyo et al. 1992). In recent decades the numbers living within towns and cities have increased greatly, with more than 1,200 breeding pairs in Kampala, supported largely by open waste disposal sites (Pomeroy and Kibuule 2017). Diet Its diet consists predominantly of carrion and scraps of fish discarded by humans as well as live fish, termites, locusts, frogs, lizards, snakes, rats, mice and birds (del Hoyo et al. 1992) (e.g. adult flamingoes Phoenicopterus spp.) (Brown et al. 1982). Breeding site The nest is constructed of sticks (del Hoyo et al. 1992) and is positioned 10-30 m above the ground in trees, on cliffs (del Hoyo et al. 1992) or on buildings in towns and villages (Brown et al. 1982). The species breeds colonially in single- or mixed-species groups (del Hoyo et al. 1992), usually in close proximity (less than 50-60 km) to a reliable food source (Hancock et al. 1992).
documentation.threats:
This species is hunted and traded at traditional medicine markets in Nigeria to the level that the species no longer breeds in the country (Nikolaus 2001, Ringim et al. 2021). It is suspected that birds are being obtained from around Lake Chad in Niger, Chad and from Cameroon to supply the trade (Ringim et al. 2021, Gula and Barlow 2023). Hunting has also been recorded in The Gambia and trade noted in Benin and Mali (Gula and Barlow 2023). The species is also persecuted by fishermen in Cameroon, who view the species as a competitor, and chicks have been recorded as being harvested from large colonies for food, causing colony abandonment (Scholte 2006). Mortality due to these drivers is suspected to have caused much of the decline and range contraction recorded in West Africa. The decline and subsequent loss as a breeding bird in Mali may be attributed to changes to the hydrological regime in the Inner Niger Delta, alongside chronic overfishing (Zwarts et al. 2009).

Loss of suitable nesting trees may impact the species' reproductive rate in parts of the range, with demand for charcoal and clearance for agriculture suspected to be causing issues for the species in The Gambia and previously in Nigeria (Gula and Barlow 2023), although motivation for cutting colony trees may actually also be hunting and persecution of the species itself. There is mortality from collision with high-voltage powerlines in the vicinity of the Kiteezi landfill site, Kampala, with 23 carcasses found over the course of a year in 2012-2013 (Kibuule and Pomeroy 2015), though this level of mortality does not seem to be sufficient to have offset the growth of this colony, which continued to increase to a peak in 2016 (Pomeroy and Kibuule 2021).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions in Place
Listed as Endangered under the Nigeria Endangered Species Act, 2016, which legislates that a permit is required for trade in the species (Ringim et al. 2021), and the Wildlife Conservation Act 1977 in The Gambia. Assessed as Near Threatened in Namibia (Simmons et al. 2015) and South Africa (Taylor et al. 2015), and Vulnerable in Eswatini (Monadjem et al. 2003).

Conservation Actions Needed
Action to address the illegal trade in fetish markets of northern Namibia is required to address severe regional declines, including programmes of poverty alleviation, education and a concurrent increase in enforcement capacity and action. These actions are also those relevant for vultures in the region.
documentation.use_trade: Species is kept widely in captivity, though there is very little breeding success reported. This species has been reported as traded at a very high prevalence, being found in five of the seven trade datasets evaluated (Donald et al. 2024). There is considerable illegal trade in Marabou Storks in Nigeria, which is believed to have been the primary driver of the loss of the species as a breeder in the country (Ringim et al. 2021). Trade is for belief-based use and is similar to that recorded for vultures, with a single Marabou estimated to be worth around USD $90 (Ringim et al. 2021). Feathers are also used to make ceremonial clothing and accessories, such as fans (Ringim et al. 2021). Harvest of chicks from large colonies for food has been reported in Cameroon (Gula and Pomeroy 2023), and has caused colony abandonment (Scholte 2006). Fine feathers of the ruff and undertail coverts were used in fashion in Europe in the early 20th century, with sufficient demand to cause the species to be very rare in Uganda, and restricted to the west of the country (Pomeroy and Kibuule 2021).
documentation.rationale: This species has an extremely large range and a moderately large to large population size. In East Africa and southern Africa, which holds the bulk of the population, it is thought to be largely stable but has increased considerably where it has adapted to living alongside people and in areas where it is free from persecution. In contrast, rapid population declines and a considerable range reduction have been recorded from West Africa, where the drivers of decline appear to have been hunting for belief-based use and for food. Overall the population is considered to be declining, but at a slow rate which does not approach threatened thresholds. For these reasons the species is evaluated as Least Concern.
documentation.trend_justification:
The population trend for the species is suspected to be decreasing at a slow rate, driven by the rapid losses recorded in West Africa (Gula and Barlow 2023). Previously the population was thought to be increasing: based on IWC data, Nagy and Langendoen (2020) reported an increasing trend (1.0644) for 1994-2017 and uncertain trend with a strong increasing tendency (1.1189) for the period of 2008-2017. However this did not account adequately for the observed reduction in the number of breeding colonies and reduction in occupied range documented in West Africa (Gula and Barlow 2023), which is considered sufficient to offset the increasing trend reported elsewhere in the range.

The rate of increase in the Gorongosa landscape has been far more rapid than would be possible from the species intrinsic rate of reproduction suggesting most is due to birds moving into the area from elsewhere (Stalmans et al. 2020). However, the high average number of nests per tree recorded is associated with greater breeding success (Pomeroy 1978, Stalmans et al. 2020), suggesting that a genuine, if slower, population increase is taking place in this region. Similarly, the increase in the colonies in Kampala is likely to have been driven by dispersal from elsewhere but then also to have seen genuine increases due to the rate of reproductive success. Drivers of increases recorded in the Okavango Delta are uncertain, however the significant change in the Delta has been a reduction in the frequency of inundation (Francis et al. 2021), while in other studies reproductive success is associated with low rainfall which is speculated to improve foraging on fish as ephemeral wetlands dry out (Monadjem et al. 2012).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Leptoptilos crumenifer (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously listed as L. crumeniferus.

conservation_actions.note: Education required to undermine the belief in the medicinal properties of Marabou Stork parts.
Enforcement of the provisions of the Nigerian Endangered Species Act in relation to the unlicensed trade in Marabou Stork parts.
